lessons.title: Devices

items.example: This keyboard has black and white keys.
items.note: Use 'keyboard' for the board with letters and numbers you press to write on a computer.

items.example: We play music on this speaker.
items.note: Say 'speaker' for the device that makes music and sounds loud and clear.

items.note: Use 'webcam' for the small camera on a computer that lets friends see you.

items.note: Say 'the internet' for the global network that connects computers and phones.

image.describe: a glowing globe surrounded by connected signal waves between a laptop and a phone

items.example: This website is interesting.

items.note: Say 'app' for a small program on a phone or tablet.

image.describe: a smartphone screen showing bright square app icons

items.example: I always remember my password.
items.note: Use 'password' for the secret letters and numbers that unlock your account.

image.describe: a lock icon next to a box with hidden stars on a tablet screen

items.example: We have a video call with Ana.

lessons.title: Messages
lessons.scenario: Zara and Smarty send Leo his science homework in the game room.

items.example: I have a new message from Leo.
items.note: Say 'message' for short written words you send on a phone or computer.

image.describe: a phone screen showing colorful speech bubbles with a new incoming message

items.example: I always send a message to my mother.
items.note: Use 'send a message' when you write to someone on your phone or app.

items.example: Please reply to my message.
items.note: Say 'reply' when you answer a message someone sent to you.

items.example: Please text me in the evening.
items.note: Say 'text me' to ask a friend to send a short phone message to you.

items.example: The photo is an attachment in my message.
items.note: Use 'attachment' for a file or photo you send together with a message.

image.describe: a paperclip icon attaching a photo card to a digital message envelope

items.example: I want to see that website. Send me a link!
items.note: Say 'Send me a link' when you want someone to message you a website address.

practice.prompt: You write words on your phone and send them to a friend. What is this?

items.note: Say 'low' when your battery power or signal is almost gone.

items.note: Say 'turn it off and on' for restarting a device to fix a small problem.

items.example: This old speaker has no music. It is broken!

lessons.title: Have you ever…?
lessons.scenario: Smarty, Mia, and Omar talk about online things they have or have not done.

items.example: Have you ever sent an attachment?
items.note: Start a question with 'Have you ever…?' to ask if someone has done something at any time in their life.

items.example: I have never bought a laptop.
items.note: Say 'I have never…' to tell someone you have not done that thing even once.

items.example: I have just sent a message to Mia.
items.note: Use 'I have just…' for an action that happened a moment ago.

items.example: Leo has already replied to my message.
items.note: Put 'already' after 'have' or 'has' to show something happened earlier than expected.

items.example: Have you sent the link yet?
items.note: Put 'yet' at the end of a question or 'not' sentence when you are waiting for something to happen.

items.example: Have you replied to Omar? — Not yet.
items.note: Answer 'Not yet' when you have not done something so far, but you plan to do it.

grammar.title: Present perfect: ever, never, just, already, yet
grammar.explanation: Use have or has with a past action word to connect past actions to now. Ask about life experience with ever, say zero times with never, show a moment ago with just, earlier than expected with already, and ask or answer about expected actions with yet and not yet.
examples: Have you ever made a video call?
I have never had a tablet.
I have just sent a message.
Have you replied yet? — Not yet.

practice.prompt: You want to ask a friend about an experience in their life. Which phrase starts the question?
practice.explanation: 'Have you ever…?' asks if something happened at any time in your life.

options: I have never bought a new laptop.
I have just bought a new laptop.

practice.explanation: Use 'yet' at the end of a question to ask if an expected action has happened.

practice.prompt: Match each expression with its time meaning.

practice.explanation: Practise asking a full 'Have you ever…?' question.
